A calculator for exactly this fitted model

Source: R/calculator.R
mm_calculator.Rd

Builds a Shiny application from the model's own prediction schema: one input per predictor, a dropdown for a categorical one offering only the levels the model was developed on, a number for a continuous one defaulting to the median the datadist recorded and stating the range it was developed on. Scoring goes through mm_predict(), so the calculator agrees with the model by construction rather than by comparison.

Usage

mm_calculator(
  model,
  title = NULL,
  subtitle = NULL,
  threshold = NULL,
  higher_is = c("worse", "better"),
  subject = "patient",
  audience = c("clinician", "self"),
  event = NULL,
  gates = NULL,
  nomogram = TRUE
)

Arguments

model

A mm_model().

title

The heading. Defaults to the outcome the model predicts.

subtitle

A line under the heading. Defaults to the project slug and the predictors.

threshold

The risk the bands are taken relative to. The default is the development cohort's own event rate, which is the only threshold a fitted model carries; a decision threshold from a decision-curve analysis belongs here when there is one. Whatever it is, the screen says so, because a band shown without the number it is relative to is not interpretable.

higher_is

Whether a higher prediction is the "worse" outcome, as it is for a complication, or the "better" one, as it is for a chance of matching. It decides which way round the colours and the gauge gradient run. The model cannot know this and the package will not guess: the default is "worse", because this is a risk calculator. The band's label stays directional either way, so the colour is never the only carrier.

subject

What one row is, in the singular. A clinical model scores a "patient", which is the default; the ENT applicant model this was first run against scores an "applicant". It is a word, not decoration: every sentence on the page uses it, and a page that calls an applicant a patient reads as though it were written for a different model.

audience

Who the page is written for: a "clinician" scoring someone else, or the "self" the row is about, reading their own prediction. It changes the instructions, which are the part of a calculator a reader is most likely to act on. An applicant reading their own chance of matching needs to be told that the model describes people who share their values rather than them; a clinician does not need that and does need to be told the number is not advice.

event

What the outcome is, in the past tense, as it would complete "of 100 applicants, 15 ___". The default is the outcome column's name, which is right when the column is named for what happened (matched) and wrong when it is not. It is read by the sentences the page writes for the person the prediction is about, where "had the outcome" is the kind of phrasing that tells a reader this page was not written for them.

gates

Inputs that another input switches off, as a named list: each name is a numeric predictor and each element gives by (the categorical predictor that controls it), when (the level at which it is switched off) and optionally value (what it reads while off, defaulting to the median the datadist recorded). A Step 2 score means nothing for an applicant who has not sat Step 2, and a form that accepts "not reported" beside a score of 250 submits a combination the model was never fitted on.

nomogram

Whether to draw the model's nomogram onto the page. The sheet comes from mm_nomogram(), so it is the verified one: it does not appear unless reading it back the way a clinician reads it reproduces mm_predict(). A model that cannot be drawn says why in place of the figure rather than leaving the panel empty.

Value

A shiny::shinyApp() object, which launches when printed.

Details

This is here because the ecosystem renderers could not be trusted with these fits. DynNom refits the model it is handed, which means the figures on screen come from coefficients re-estimated on whatever rows it recovered and not from the ones that were reported. regplot has no data argument at all. Both, together with emmeans, marginaleffects, effects and sjPlot, also fail outright on a mm_model() because the formula is built in an empty environment and carries no cohort to recover: see DEC-015 and inst/capability-matrix.md. A front end over mm_predict() reads the stored coefficients, refuses an unseen level by name and marks a row outside the development range, which is the behaviour a clinical calculator needs.

No uncertainty range is shown beside the risk. mm_predict() computes one and this function still receives it, so nothing statistical was removed, but it is not displayed: it is parameter uncertainty on the probability scale, and a reader shown it beside one person's risk would reasonably take it for the range that person's own risk lies in, which is a wider quantity this package does not compute. The three uncertainties are distinguished in the panel's own "Before you use this" text, and the interval remains in the returned prediction and in each saved record for anyone doing statistics rather than reading the screen.

This is the owner's resolution of review finding D-1, recorded in review/findings.csv. Before it, this paragraph claimed no interval was shown because mm_predict() does not produce one; both halves of that were false, and the interval was in fact rendered in three places. A regression test now fails if any of them returns.

Examples

cohort <- mm_synthetic_cohort(n = 300, seed = 1)
project <- mm_project("uds", "event", c("age", "bmi", "sex"),
                      cohort = cohort)
fit <- mm_model(project, cohort)
#> Warning: the development sample may be too small for this model: 300 rows is 26685 short of the 26985 a model of 3 parameter(s) needs at 9.3% prevalence for 90% shrinkage. Coefficients from a sample this size are expected to be overfitted; see the adequacy element of the returned object.
if (interactive() && requireNamespace("shiny", quietly = TRUE)) {
  mm_calculator(fit)
}
